title: The Bell That Rang Too Soon
passage:
At Midori Junior High, a short bell rang five minutes before the end of lunch. It was meant to remind students to finish eating and return trays before afternoon classes. For years, nobody questioned it. One month, however, the bell began ringing seven minutes early because the timer was accidentally changed during maintenance.

At first, most students simply followed the sound. They stood up, returned their trays, and left the lunch area earlier than usual. Teachers noticed that the hallway became crowded sooner, but they did not know why. A student named Reina finally looked at the wall clock and realized that the bell was not matching the schedule. She told a teacher, who checked the timer and found the error.

The simple mistake started a larger conversation. Reina's class wondered why everyone had obeyed the bell without checking the time. Some students said they trusted school signals because they were usually correct. Others admitted that they rarely looked at the clock during lunch. Their teacher said that routines are useful because they save mental effort, but routines can also make people stop noticing small changes.

For one week, the class paid attention to other automatic habits. They found that many students always used the same staircase even when another one was less crowded. Some threw paper into the nearest bin without checking whether it was for recycling. A few students opened their phones as soon as they sat down on the bus, even when they had not planned to use them. None of these habits were serious problems, but the students enjoyed noticing them.

After the timer was fixed, the bell once again rang at the correct time. Nothing about lunch changed in a dramatic way. Still, Reina began looking at the clock before standing up. She did not decide that routines were bad. Instead, she learned to treat them as helpful tools rather than unquestioned commands. A familiar signal can guide us efficiently, but every so often it is worth checking whether the signal still matches reality.
translation:
緑中学校では、昼休み終了の五分前に短いベルが鳴っていました。食事を終え、トレーを返し、午後の授業へ戻る準備をする合図です。長年、誰も特に疑問を持ちませんでした。ところがある月、点検の際にタイマー設定が変わり、ベルが七分も早く鳴るようになりました。

最初、生徒たちの多くは音に従い、いつもより早く立ってトレーを返しました。廊下が早い時間から混み始めましたが、先生たちは理由が分かりませんでした。レイナが壁時計を見て初めて、ベルと時刻が合っていないことに気づきました。先生が確認すると設定ミスが見つかりました。

この小さな失敗をきっかけに、『なぜ誰も時計を確認しなかったのか』という話になりました。学校の合図は普段正しいので信頼していたという生徒もいれば、昼休みに時計をほとんど見ないという生徒もいました。先生は、習慣は考える負担を減らしてくれる一方、変化に気づきにくくすることもあると説明しました。

クラスは一週間、他の無意識の習慣も観察しました。別の階段の方が空いていてもいつも同じ階段を使う、分別表示を確認せず一番近いごみ箱へ紙を入れる、使う予定がなくてもバスで座るとすぐスマートフォンを開く、といった行動が見つかりました。重大な問題ではありませんでしたが、気づくこと自体が面白かったのです。

タイマーが直ると、ベルは再び正しい時刻に鳴るようになりました。大きな変化はありませんでしたが、レイナは立つ前に時計を見るようになりました。習慣そのものが悪いのではありません。便利な道具として使い、ときどき現実と合っているか確かめることが大切だと学んだのです。

title: Seeds on the Balcony
passage:
When Yuta's family moved to an apartment, he missed the small garden beside their old house. The new home had no yard, only a narrow balcony that received morning sunlight. Yuta assumed that growing vegetables would no longer be possible. His mother suggested trying a few pots before giving up.

They began with lettuce, radishes, and small tomatoes. Yuta filled containers with soil and carefully followed the instructions on the seed packets. During the first week, nothing seemed to happen. He checked the pots every morning and wondered whether the seeds were bad. Then tiny green leaves appeared. They were so small that he almost missed them.

The balcony created new problems. Wind dried the soil faster than it had in the old garden, and one container received too much water during heavy rain. The tomato plant also leaned toward the railing because it was searching for sunlight. Yuta and his mother moved the pots, added simple supports, and made small holes so extra water could escape. They discovered that growing plants in a limited space required different methods, not less care.

By early summer, they could pick lettuce for sandwiches and several red radishes. The tomatoes took longer. Yuta became impatient because the green fruit seemed unchanged for days. His mother told him that checking every hour would not make them ripen faster. When the first tomato finally turned red, he waited one extra day before picking it. The taste was not especially different from tomatoes sold in a store, but he felt proud because he knew every step that had brought it to the plate.

The balcony never became a real garden in the old sense. There was no grass, no tree, and not enough space to grow many plants. Yet Yuta stopped thinking of it as a poor replacement. It was simply a different kind of growing place. He learned that losing one condition does not always mean losing the activity itself. Sometimes the activity can survive if people are willing to change the way they do it.
translation:
ユウタの家族が集合住宅へ引っ越したとき、彼は以前の家の横にあった小さな庭が恋しくなりました。新居には庭がなく、朝日が当たる細いベランダしかありません。野菜作りはもうできないと思っていましたが、母は諦める前に鉢で試してみようと提案しました。

レタス、ラディッシュ、ミニトマトから始め、種袋の説明をよく読んで植えました。一週目は何も起きないように見えましたが、やがて見落としそうなほど小さな緑の芽が出ました。

ベランダには庭とは違う問題がありました。風で土が早く乾き、大雨では水がたまり、トマトは日光を求めて手すり側へ傾きました。鉢の位置を変え、支柱を立て、余分な水が抜ける穴を作ることで対応しました。狭い場所では世話が少なくなるのではなく、方法が変わるのだと分かりました。

初夏にはサンドイッチ用のレタスや赤いラディッシュを収穫できました。トマトは時間がかかり、ユウタは待ちきれませんでしたが、母から何度見ても早く熟すわけではないと言われました。最初の実が赤くなったとき、あえてもう一日待ってから取りました。店のトマトと特別違う味ではありませんでしたが、皿に届くまでのすべての過程を知っていることが誇らしく感じられました。

ベランダは昔の庭と同じにはなりませんでした。芝生も木もなく、多くの植物を育てる広さもありません。それでもユウタは『劣った代用品』とは考えなくなりました。条件が一つ失われても、やり方を変えれば活動そのものは続けられることがあると学んだのです。

title: A Book Returned Ten Years Late
passage:
One rainy afternoon, the town library received a package with no return address. Inside was a children's science book, an old library card, and a short letter. The book had been borrowed almost ten years earlier. The writer explained that her family had moved suddenly, and the book had been packed into a box by mistake. She had recently found it while cleaning a storage room.

The librarian, Mr. Ono, checked the computer system. The old loan record was no longer active, and the library did not charge large late fees for children's books. He was more interested in the condition of the book. The cover was worn, but all the pages were there. Someone had placed a small paper star between two pages as a bookmark.

The letter said that the writer had loved the book as a child because it explained simple experiments with light, water, and magnets. She remembered trying several experiments at home. Years later, she became a science teacher. She did not claim that one book had decided her future, but she believed it had helped her become curious about how ordinary things worked. She apologized for keeping it for so long and hoped another child could read it.

Mr. Ono showed the letter to the other library staff. They repaired the cover and placed the book on a display table with a copy of the letter. They removed the writer's name for privacy. The display was called ‘A Book Comes Home.’ Children stopped to read the story, and several asked whether the experiments in the book still worked. One librarian tested them and confirmed that most were still safe and useful.

A month later, the book returned to the regular shelf. It was no longer new or especially attractive, but it was borrowed often. Mr. Ono liked that the book now carried two kinds of value. It contained science information, but it also reminded readers that books can travel through people's lives in unexpected ways. Returning something late was not ideal, yet the return itself created a new story for the library.
translation:
雨の日の午後、町の図書館に差出人のない小包が届きました。中には子ども向け科学本、古い図書カード、短い手紙が入っていました。その本はほぼ十年前に借りられたもので、家族が急に引っ越した際、間違って箱へ入れたままになっていたそうです。最近、物置を片付けていて見つけたと書かれていました。

司書の小野さんが調べると、古い貸出記録はすでに現在のシステムでは使われておらず、子どもの本に高額な延滞金を課すこともありませんでした。表紙は傷んでいましたが、ページはそろっており、紙で作った小さな星のしおりも残っていました。

手紙には、その本が光、水、磁石を使った簡単な実験を紹介していて、子どもの頃にとても好きだったことが書かれていました。家でいくつか試し、のちに科学教師になったそうです。一冊の本だけが将来を決めたとは思わないけれど、身近なものの仕組みに興味を持つ助けになったと感じていました。長い間返せなかったことを謝り、別の子にも読んでほしいと書かれていました。

図書館は表紙を修理し、名前を伏せた手紙のコピーと一緒に『本が帰ってきた』という展示を作りました。子どもたちは立ち止まって話を読み、本の実験が今でもできるのか尋ねました。司書が確認すると、多くは今でも安全に試せる内容でした。

一か月後、本は普通の棚へ戻りました。新しくも派手でもありませんが、よく借りられるようになりました。小野さんは、その本には二つの価値があると感じました。科学の知識だけでなく、本が人の人生の中を思いがけず旅することを示していたからです。返却が十年遅れたこと自体は良いことではありませんが、その返却が図書館に新しい物語を生みました。

title: The Path Behind the Station
passage:
For years, people leaving Sakura Station used the main road to reach the shopping street. The route was safe, but it took almost fifteen minutes because pedestrians had to walk around a large parking area. Behind the station there was a narrower path beside a fence. Local residents knew it, but visitors rarely used it because the entrance looked private.

A group of high school students noticed the problem while studying local transportation. They timed both routes and found that the narrow path saved about six minutes. However, they also saw why people avoided it. There was no sign, weeds covered part of the entrance, and one section became muddy after rain. The students decided that simply telling people about the shortcut would not be enough.

They spoke with the landowner, the station manager, and the city office. To their surprise, the path was already public, but responsibility for maintenance had not been clear. The city agreed to remove weeds and add gravel to the muddy section. The station placed a small sign saying ‘Public Walking Route to Shopping Street.’ The students drew a simple map and asked several visitors to try the route.

Most people found it easily after seeing the sign. An older man, however, said the gravel was difficult to walk on with his cane. The students reported this, and a narrow smooth strip was added along one side. The path was still not suitable for bicycles, and it could not replace the main road for everyone, but it became a useful option for many pedestrians.

The students were proud of the result because they had not built anything large. Their most important work had been noticing an existing route, finding out why it was underused, and connecting the people who could improve it. The project showed them that solving a local problem does not always require creating something new. Sometimes a useful resource is already there, waiting to be made clearer, safer, and easier to reach.
translation:
さくら駅から商店街へ行く人は長年、正面の大通りを使っていました。安全ですが、大きな駐車場を回り込むため約十五分かかります。駅の裏には柵沿いの細い道があり、地元の人は知っていましたが、入口が私有地のように見えるため訪問者はほとんど使いませんでした。

地域交通を調べていた高校生が二つの経路を計ると、細い道なら約六分短縮できました。ただし、案内表示がなく、入口に雑草があり、雨の後にぬかるむ場所もありました。近道だと教えるだけでは不十分だと考えました。

土地所有者、駅、市役所へ聞くと、実はその道は公共の通路でしたが、管理の責任が曖昧になっていました。市が雑草を取り、泥になる場所に砂利を入れ、駅は『商店街への公共歩行路』という小さな表示を設置しました。生徒たちは地図も作り、訪問者に試してもらいました。

多くの人は使いやすいと答えましたが、杖を使う年配男性から砂利は歩きにくいという意見が出ました。そこで片側に細い平らな部分が追加されました。自転車には向かず、全員が大通りの代わりに使えるわけではありませんが、多くの歩行者には便利な選択肢になりました。

生徒たちは大きな建物を作ったわけではありません。すでにある道に気づき、なぜ使われていないか調べ、改善できる人たちをつないだことが成果でした。地域の問題は必ずしも新しいものを作らなければ解決できないわけではなく、すでにある資源を分かりやすく、安全で、利用しやすくすることでも解決できると学びました。

title: A Classroom With No Clock
passage:
When the wall clock in Class 2-B stopped working, the teacher planned to replace the battery after school. Before she could do it, one student suggested leaving the clock broken for a day. The class laughed, but the teacher agreed as long as lessons were not interrupted. Students still had watches, tablets, and the school bell, so nobody would truly lose track of time.

The next morning, the blank clock face became surprisingly noticeable. Several students looked up at it automatically during the first lesson and then remembered that it was useless. Others checked the time on a tablet instead. During group work, one student kept asking how many minutes were left because she could no longer glance at the wall.

At lunch, the class discussed what they had noticed. Some students said the clock helped them plan. If ten minutes remained, they knew whether to begin a new task. Others said they looked at it too often, especially during difficult lessons. One boy admitted that seeing only five minutes pass sometimes made a class feel slower. Without the clock, he had focused more on finishing the work in front of him.

The teacher used a small timer for activities that needed exact limits, but she did not announce every minute. By the end of the day, students had different opinions. A few wanted the wall clock removed permanently, while most preferred to have it back. The class decided the useful question was not whether clocks were good or bad. It was how often they needed time information and when checking it became a distraction.

The next morning, the clock had a new battery. Students could once again see the time with a glance. Yet for several days, some of them noticed themselves before looking up. That brief pause was the most lasting result of the experiment. The broken clock had made a common object visible by taking away its normal function. It reminded the class that tools can guide behavior so quietly that people may not notice the guidance until the tool disappears.
translation:
2年B組の壁時計が止まったとき、先生は放課後に電池を替えるつもりでした。ところが生徒の一人が、一日だけ壊れたままにしてみようと提案しました。授業を妨げないことを条件に先生も同意しました。腕時計やタブレット、校内ベルがあるので、本当に時間が分からなくなるわけではありません。

翌朝、動かない時計は意外なほど気になりました。何人もの生徒が第一時限中に無意識に見上げ、そのたびに使えないことを思い出しました。グループ活動では、壁を一目見れば済まないため、残り時間を何度も尋ねる生徒もいました。

昼休みに感想を話すと、時計は計画に役立つという意見がありました。残り十分なら次の作業を始めるか判断できます。一方、難しい授業では時計を見すぎるという生徒もいました。五分しか進んでいないのを見ると、授業が長く感じることがあるというのです。時計がない方が目の前の作業へ集中できたとも話しました。

正確な時間制限が必要な活動では先生が小さなタイマーを使いました。最終的に、壁時計をなくしたい生徒も少数いましたが、多くは戻してほしいと考えました。大切なのは時計が良いか悪いかではなく、いつ時間情報が必要で、いつ確認が気を散らすのかという問いでした。

翌朝、時計には新しい電池が入りました。それでも数日間、何人かは見上げる直前に自分の行動へ気づくようになりました。これが実験の一番長く残った変化でした。普段当たり前の道具は、その働きを失ったとき初めて、どれほど静かに行動を導いていたか見えてくることがあります。

title: The Umbrella Shelf
passage:
On rainy days, the entrance of Hikari Community Center became crowded with wet umbrellas. There was one large umbrella stand, but many umbrellas looked similar. People often spent several minutes searching when they left, and once in a while someone accidentally took the wrong one. The staff considered putting numbered tags on every umbrella, but that would require someone to manage the tags all day.

A volunteer named Mari suggested a simpler idea. Instead of one large stand, they could divide umbrellas into several groups. The center already had an unused wooden shelf with six sections. They placed a waterproof tray under it and labeled the sections with easy pictures: sun, moon, tree, bird, fish, and star. Visitors could choose any section and remember the picture.

The first rainy day showed one problem. Most children wanted to use the star and bird sections, so those became crowded while other spaces stayed empty. The staff changed the sign. It now asked visitors to use the least crowded section. They also placed a small card at the reception desk with the six pictures so people could point to the one they had chosen if they forgot its name.

The new system did not completely prevent mistakes. Two identical black umbrellas were still confused one afternoon. After that, Mari added a basket of reusable colored bands that visitors could loosely wrap around a handle. The bands were not required, but they helped people with common umbrella designs.

By the end of the rainy season, the entrance was easier to use. The solution had cost almost nothing because the center reused a shelf and simple materials it already owned. Mari liked the project because it showed that organization can solve a problem even when technology is unnecessary. The center did not need a digital ticket machine or a complicated rule. It needed a way to break one crowded space into smaller, memorable choices. Sometimes a simple picture is enough to make a shared place work better.
translation:
雨の日、ひかり公民館の入口は濡れた傘で混雑していました。大きな傘立てが一つありましたが、似た傘が多く、帰る時に探すのに時間がかかり、ときには間違えて持ち帰る人もいました。番号札を付ける案も出ましたが、一日中管理する人が必要になります。

ボランティアのマリは、傘をいくつかのグループに分けるという単純な方法を提案しました。使っていない六区画の木製棚に防水トレーを置き、太陽、月、木、鳥、魚、星の絵を付けました。来館者は好きな区画へ入れ、その絵を覚えます。

最初の雨の日、子どもたちが星と鳥へ集中し、そこだけ混雑しました。そこで『一番空いている区画を使ってください』と表示を変え、受付には六つの絵のカードを置き、名前を忘れても指させるようにしました。

完全に間違いがなくなったわけではありません。同じ黒い傘が取り違えられたこともあり、持ち手へ軽く巻ける再利用可能な色バンドを追加しました。必須ではありませんが、よく似た傘の区別に役立ちました。

梅雨の終わりには入口が使いやすくなっていました。古い棚と手元の材料を再利用したため費用はほとんどかかりませんでした。マリは、この計画から、技術を使わなくても『整理の仕方』で問題を解けることがあると学びました。複雑な機械ではなく、一つの混雑した場所を覚えやすい小さな選択肢へ分けるだけでよかったのです。

title: The Empty Notice Board
passage:
Near the entrance of Keiko's school stood a large notice board. It had once been used for club announcements, but most information had moved online. The board was usually empty except for old tape marks and one faded safety poster. Students passed it every day without looking.

During a class discussion about communication, Keiko wondered whether the board could still be useful. Not every message needed to be urgent or digital. Her group suggested turning it into a space for small local information. Their teacher agreed, but asked them to make clear rules so the board would not become messy.

The students divided the board into four sections: school events, community events, lost and found, and ‘something worth sharing.’ Every notice needed a date, and old notices would be removed after two weeks. The last section was the most unusual. Students could post a short recommendation for a book, a walking route, a museum, or even a useful study method. Advertisements for products were not allowed.

At first, only a few notices appeared. Then a student posted a hand-drawn map showing a safe bicycle route around road construction. Another recommended a free weekend concert at the city hall. Someone wrote a short note about a quiet place in the library that had more power outlets. The board slowly became colorful, but it did not become crowded because expired notices were removed regularly.

Keiko noticed that the board offered something different from online messages. People saw information they had not searched for. A student walking to class might discover a concert, a lost pencil case, or a book recommendation by accident. The board was slower than a phone and could not send reminders, but its physical location created chance encounters with information.

By the end of the term, the board was no longer empty. Keiko learned that an old tool does not always become useless when a newer one appears. Sometimes its role simply changes. The board could not compete with the speed of online communication, yet it could provide a shared place where unexpected information became visible.
translation:
ケイコの学校の入口近くには大きな掲示板がありました。以前は部活動の案内に使われていましたが、多くの情報がオンラインへ移り、古いテープ跡と色あせた安全ポスターが残るだけになっていました。生徒たちは毎日その前を通っても見ようとしませんでした。

連絡手段について授業で話し合った際、ケイコは掲示板にもまだ役割があるのではないかと考えました。すべての情報が緊急でもデジタルでもありません。グループは地域の小さな情報を集める場所にすることを提案しました。先生は賛成しましたが、散らからないようルールを決めるよう求めました。

掲示板を『学校行事』『地域行事』『落とし物』『おすすめ』の四区画に分け、すべての掲示に日付を入れ、二週間で外すことにしました。おすすめ欄には、本、散歩道、博物館、勉強方法などを書けますが、商品の広告は禁止しました。

最初は少数でしたが、工事を避ける安全な自転車ルートの手描き地図、無料コンサート、図書館でコンセントが多い静かな場所などが貼られ、徐々に色彩が増えました。期限切れを外すので混雑しませんでした。

ケイコは、掲示板にはオンラインと違う良さがあると気づきました。人は検索していなかった情報に偶然出会えます。スマートフォンほど速くなく通知もできませんが、同じ場所を通る人の目に予想外の情報を届けられます。

学期末、掲示板はもう空ではありませんでした。新しい道具が現れたからといって、古い道具が必ず無価値になるわけではありません。役割が変わることがあります。掲示板はネットの速度には勝てませんが、思いがけない情報が目に入る共有の場所として役立ちました。

title: The Morning Market List
passage:
Every Saturday, Hana went to the morning market with her father. They often bought vegetables, fish, bread, and fruit. Her father enjoyed talking with the sellers, but Hana thought shopping took too long. One week she suggested making a strict list and following it without stopping. Her father agreed to try.

The next Saturday, Hana wrote six items on a piece of paper. They bought the first four quickly. At the fifth stall, however, a farmer said the spinach on Hana's list had been damaged by heavy rain and was not available. He suggested a local leafy vegetable that Hana had never eaten. Her list did not include it, so she wanted to move on, but her father asked how it could be cooked.

The farmer explained that it could be added to soup or lightly fried with sesame oil. Hana's father bought one bunch. At another stall, the apples on the list were expensive because the local crop was small that week. The seller recommended pears instead. Hana realized that a market changed from week to week in ways a fixed list could not predict.

At home, they cooked the unfamiliar vegetable in soup. Hana liked it more than she expected. She still believed lists were useful. Without one, her father sometimes forgot important things and bought too much bread. But she changed the way she used the list. The next week, she divided it into two parts: ‘must buy’ and ‘can change.’ Rice and eggs were in the first group, while fruit and leafy vegetables were in the second.

Shopping became easier without becoming completely rigid. Hana could move quickly when the plan worked and adjust when the market offered something different. She learned that planning and flexibility were not opposites. A good plan can include places where change is allowed. In fact, knowing which parts are fixed and which parts can move may make a plan stronger, not weaker.
translation:
毎週土曜日、ハナは父と朝市へ行き、野菜、魚、パン、果物などを買っていました。父は店の人との会話を楽しみましたが、ハナは買い物に時間がかかりすぎると思っていました。そこで厳密なリストを作り、寄り道せず買おうと提案しました。

翌週、六品を書いた紙を持って行き、最初の四品はすぐ買えました。ところが五つ目のほうれん草は大雨で収穫が少なく、代わりにハナが食べたことのない地元野菜を勧められました。リスト外なので通り過ぎたかったのですが、父が調理法を尋ね、スープやごま油炒めにできると聞いて一束買いました。

別の店では、地元の収穫が少なくリンゴが高く、代わりに梨を勧められました。ハナは、市場は毎週変わり、固定したリストでは予測できないことがあると気づきました。

家で新しい野菜をスープにすると、思った以上においしく感じました。リストが不要だと思ったわけではありません。父はリストがないと大事な物を忘れたりパンを買いすぎたりするからです。次の週、ハナは『必ず買う物』と『変えてよい物』の二つに分けました。米と卵は前者、果物や葉物野菜は後者です。

すると計画性を保ちながら柔軟に買い物できました。計画と柔軟さは反対ではありません。良い計画には『変更してよい場所』を含めることができます。どこを固定し、どこを動かせるか分かっている方が、むしろ計画は強くなることがあるのです。

title: A Chair for Everyone
passage:
The art room at Takumi's school had twenty-four stools and two regular chairs. Most students used the stools without thinking about them. During an open class, however, a visitor with an injured leg found it difficult to sit safely. The teacher brought one of the regular chairs, but it was stored in another room and took time to find.

After the event, the class discussed whether the art room needed different seating. Buying twenty-four new chairs would be expensive and unnecessary. The stools were useful because they could be stacked and moved easily. Instead, the students tried to understand what kinds of situations required another option. They asked the school nurse and spoke with students who had temporarily used crutches after sports injuries.

They learned that a backrest was helpful for some people, and armrests could make standing up easier. Space was also important because a large chair placed between crowded art tables might create a new problem. The class decided to keep most stools and add three stable chairs with backs. One chair also had armrests. They marked a small storage area so the chairs would always be easy to find.

A few months later, one student hurt her ankle and used one of the chairs for two weeks. Another student sometimes chose a chair because of back pain. The chairs were not reserved only for people with visible injuries. The teacher explained that anyone who needed a different seat could use one without having to give a long reason.

Takumi found that the room still looked almost the same. There had been no large renovation, yet the space worked better for more people. He learned that making a place accessible does not always mean replacing everything with one ‘perfect’ design. Sometimes variety is more useful. Different people, and even the same person on different days, may need different things. A room can become more welcoming simply by offering more than one way to use it.
translation:
タクミの学校の美術室には、二十四脚の丸椅子と普通の椅子が二脚ありました。普段は誰も気にしませんでしたが、公開授業の日、足をけがした来場者が安全に座りにくい場面がありました。先生が別室から背もたれ付きの椅子を持ってきましたが、探すのに時間がかかりました。

授業後、すべての椅子を買い替える必要があるのか話し合いました。丸椅子は積み重ねられ移動しやすい利点があります。そこで、どんな時に別の座席が必要なのかを保健室や松葉杖を使った経験のある生徒へ聞きました。

背もたれが役立つ人がいること、立ち上がる際にひじ掛けが助けになる場合があること、そして大きな椅子を狭い机の間へ置くと別の問題が生まれることが分かりました。そこで丸椅子は残し、背もたれ付きの安定した椅子を三脚追加し、そのうち一脚にはひじ掛けを付けました。保管位置も決め、いつでも見つけられるようにしました。

数か月後、足首を痛めた生徒が二週間利用し、腰痛のある生徒も時々使いました。目に見えるけがの人だけの専用品にはせず、必要なら長い説明をしなくても使えるようにしました。

美術室の見た目はほとんど変わっていませんが、より多くの人が使いやすくなりました。利用しやすい空間を作ることは、すべてを一つの『完璧な形』へ変えることではない場合があります。人によって、また同じ人でも日によって必要なものは違います。複数の使い方を用意するだけで、場所はより受け入れやすくなるのです。

title: The Sound of the Old Piano
passage:
In the corner of the assembly hall stood an old upright piano. It was used only a few times each year because the music room had newer instruments. Some keys were slightly yellow, and the wooden surface had small scratches. When the school began discussing whether to remove unused furniture, the piano was placed on the list.

Before a decision was made, a music teacher named Ms. Kato asked for one week. She knew the piano was old, but she wanted to learn whether it was truly useless. A piano technician inspected it and found that the instrument needed tuning and two small repairs. The cost was much lower than buying a new piano, though still high enough that the school needed a reason to keep it.

Ms. Kato opened the hall during lunch for three days and invited students to play. She expected only music club members, but other students came too. One boy played a song he had learned from his grandmother. A student who usually practiced on a digital keyboard said the old piano felt different because the keys responded to how strongly she pressed them. Several students simply sat and listened.

The school then learned something unexpected. A former student visiting for a sports event recognized the piano. He remembered using it in a graduation ceremony twenty-five years earlier. He sent a message to classmates, and several replied with similar memories. The piano was not valuable because it was rare or expensive. It was valuable because many people connected it with events in the school's history.

The school decided to repair and keep it, but not as a museum object. Students were encouraged to use it during lunch and small events. The decision did not mean every old object should be saved. Storage space and repair costs still mattered. Yet the piano taught the school to ask one more question before throwing something away: not only ‘Do we use this now?’ but also ‘Could this still have a useful or meaningful role?’ Sometimes an old object can continue by finding a new purpose.
translation:
講堂の隅に古いアップライトピアノがありました。音楽室には新しい楽器があるため年に数回しか使われず、鍵盤は少し黄ばみ、木部にも傷がありました。学校が使われていない家具の整理を始めたとき、処分候補に入りました。

決定前に加藤先生が一週間待ってほしいと頼みました。本当に使えないのか確かめたかったのです。調律師が調べると、調律と二か所の小修理で使えることが分かりました。新品よりはるかに安いものの、修理費を出すには残す理由が必要でした。

先生は三日間、昼休みに講堂を開き、自由に弾いてよいことにしました。音楽部だけでなく、祖母から教わった曲を弾く男子生徒や、普段デジタル鍵盤を使う生徒も来ました。古いピアノは押す強さで鍵盤の反応が変わると感じたそうです。弾かずに聞くだけの生徒もいました。

さらに、スポーツ行事で来校した卒業生がピアノに気づき、二十五年前の卒業式で使ったことを覚えていました。同級生へ知らせると、同じような思い出がいくつも返ってきました。珍しい高価な楽器だから価値があるのではなく、多くの人が学校の出来事と結び付けていたのです。

学校は修理して残すことにしましたが、展示物にはせず、昼休みや小さな行事で使えるようにしました。すべての古い物を保存すべきだという意味ではありません。場所や費用も重要です。ただし捨てる前に『今使っているか』だけでなく、『これから別の役割を持てるか』も考える価値があると学びました。古い物でも、新しい役割を見つければ続いていけることがあります。
